us-house.budget-law-enforcement: a budget law that put funding for immigration enforcement and border barriers worth about 0.6 percent of one year's economic output, mostly to be spent across four years, that multiplies yearly spending on immigration detention by about four, and that creates new fees for asylum applications, work permits for asylum seekers, and temporary protection from removal
us-house.detention-mandate-law: a law obliging immigration authorities to hold in detention residents without legal status who are charged with theft, burglary, shoplifting, or assaulting a police officer, even without a conviction. Immigration authorities put its cost in the first year at about 0.1 percent of annual economic output
us-house.enforcement-funding-law: a budget law that adds immigration enforcement funding worth about 0.23 percent of one year's economic output, spent over roughly three years, chiefly on hiring enforcement officers and on enforcement operations
us-house.protected-status-bill: a bill obliging the government to keep, for three more years, the temporary protection from removal and the work permits of about 350,000 people from one country, about 0.1 percent of the population, which the government had moved to end

uk-commons.work-visa-rules: rule changes that close work visas to care workers recruited from abroad and require degree-level skills for other work visas. By the government's estimate, about 12,000 to 15,000 fewer work visas are issued each year, about 0.02 percent of the population
uk-commons.asylum-bill: a bill that limits the right to family and private life in immigration cases, merges refugee status and humanitarian protection into one status with set grounds for revoking it, and makes asylum seekers repay support once they can. By the government's estimate, about 14,000 more applications a year to stay on family or private-life grounds are refused, about 0.02 percent of the population
uk-commons.settlement-wait-decision: a decision that doubles the usual wait for migrants to settle permanently from five years to ten, sets waits of twenty years or more for refugees on the main protection route and for people who have drawn public benefits, and shortens the wait for high earners. By the government's estimate, more than 500,000 people, about 0.7 percent of the population, would qualify to settle later over five years than under the earlier rules

de-bundestag.family-reunification-suspension: a law halting for two years, outside cases of hardship, family reunification for people holding subsidiary protection, a route that had allowed about 12,000 visas a year, about 0.01 percent of the population

fr-assemblee.territory-birthright-law: a law under which a child born to foreign parents in one overseas territory becomes a citizen only if both parents, rather than one, had lived in the country legally for at least a year, rather than three months, at the time of birth. Under the earlier rule, about 1,577 minors a year, about 0.002 percent of the population, had become citizens
fr-assemblee.detention-210-law: a law letting immigration detention last up to 210 days instead of 90 for foreigners under removal orders who are judged a particularly serious threat to public order

ca-commons.levels-plan: a three-year immigration plan setting the coming year's new temporary residents at about 0.9 percent of the population, 43 percent below the previous year's target, and keeping new permanent residents at about 0.9 percent of the population a year, about 4 percent below the previous year's target
ca-commons.borders-act: a law that stops asylum claims from being referred to a hearing when made more than a year after the person first arrived, or more than 14 days after crossing the land border away from official crossings, and that lets the government cancel, suspend, or halt processing of groups of immigration documents and applications
ca-commons.citizenship-descent-law: a law that extends citizenship by descent past the first generation to children born abroad if the citizen parent had spent at least three years in total in the country before the birth, and gives it back to people shut out by the earlier one-generation limit. Official estimates of those affected ran from tens of thousands to about 115,000, up to about 0.3 percent of the population
ca-commons.permanent-residence-measure: a one-time measure in the coming year's immigration plan that grants permanent residence to up to 200,000 temporary residents already in the country, about 0.5 percent of the population, without changing yearly targets
